case_study_insert.main_stem: Kestrel Brook Vineyards (KBV) is a private limited company in the wine and beverage sector, employing a workforce of 40. Founded in 2007 by Rowan Kestrel, it now supplies bottled wine to national supermarket chains and operates a flat organisational structure with democratic leadership. KBV plans to invest $720,000 in a new irrigation system and automated bottling line, financed by a $450,000 ten-year bank loan and $270,000 of retained profit. It has fixed costs of $245,000 a year, a variable cost of $9.20 a unit and a selling price of $16.20, and currently produces 60,000 units a year for its retail customers. KBV faces two operational problems: bottling-line defects of 2.4% and labour turnover of 9%.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Operations and Quality Report — Q3 2025: The vineyard bottled 15,000 units last quarter at a defect rate of 2.4%, down from 3.6% a year ago. Customer complaints fell from 31 to 17 a month. Average order fulfilment is 4.1 days. Market research of 500 shoppers found that 68% would pay up to $0.50 more for sustainably bottled wine and 47% check bottle recycling before buying. A training-needs analysis shows 12 of 40 staff have not completed on-the-job training on the new bottling machines; off-the-job training courses at the local college cost $800 per employee.

appendix_2_financial_data.title: Extract from the Statement of Financial Position of Kestrel Brook Vineyards as at 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank has raised the base interest rate from 4.25% to 5.0%, increasing borrowing costs for businesses with variable-rate loans. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 5.8% from $13.00 to $13.75 per hour from April 2026, raising total wage bills. (3) Glass and cork input costs have risen 9.3% year-on-year, beverage-price inflation is 6.4%, while consumer spending on premium wine grew 3.5% in the same period.

questions.question_text: KBV plans to fund part of its bottling-line expansion with a ten-year bank loan. Explain two advantages for KBV of using retained profit instead of the bank loan.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Retained profit is internally generated, so KBV pays no interest or capital repayments on the $270,000 used for the new irrigation system and automated bottling line. With fixed costs of $245,000 a year and a $450,000 bank loan already outstanding, avoiding another debt-service charge protects cash flow and the $7.00 contribution earned on each of 60,000 bottles. Every dollar saved in interest can instead absorb the 9.3% rise in glass and cork input costs, helping KBV hold its $16.20 selling price for national supermarket chains.

Point 2: Using retained profit keeps ownership and control with founder Rowan Kestrel and the existing shareholders. A further bank loan could impose covenants and, if the 2.4% bottling defects persisted and sales slipped, the lender could demand repayment or secure company assets, putting the whole $720,000 investment at risk. Retained profit carries no such condition, so the flat, democratic management team can decide how to run the new line without external pressure, while the existing $450,000 facility stays available for working capital and the 9% labour-turnover problem can be addressed with training.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage of retained profit over a bank loan (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation applied to KBV's $270,000 retained profit, $450,000 loan, costs and defects.

questions.question_text: KBV is launching its new sustainably bottled wine range. Consider a national television campaign, local radio sponsorship, or social media influencer marketing. Which should KBV choose to promote the launch? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
National television campaign: A nationwide TV campaign would build brand awareness quickly across all the supermarket chains stocking KBV's wine and could reach millions of buyers in one flight. The drawbacks are decisive for a 40-employee vineyard: airtime and production costs are very high relative to $245,000 fixed costs, and much of the audience drinks no premium wine or lives outside the distribution network, so spend is wasted. Funding it would also compete with the $450,000 bank loan repayments on the $720,000 bottling investment.

Local radio sponsorship: Regional radio is much cheaper, targets KBV's core local catchment and suits time-sensitive messages about a new launch. Its reach is narrow, however; KBV supplies national supermarket chains and needs volume to sell 60,000 units a year, so regional listeners alone cannot create the demand required. It also cannot showcase the visual story of sustainable bottling as well as digital media.

Social media influencer marketing: Food and lifestyle influencers can demonstrate the sustainable bottles directly to the 68% of 500 surveyed shoppers willing to pay up to $0.50 more and the 47% who check recycling, with measurable engagement at low cost per reached shopper and national reach. Results build more slowly than TV and depend on influencer credibility, but this option precisely matches the research evidence.

Recommendation: KBV should choose social media influencer marketing. It reaches the exact identified segment, costs far less than television, scales nationally unlike radio, and supports the premium price needed for a $7.00 contribution per unit. Television is rejected as unaffordable and untargeted; radio is rejected as too narrow for national supermarket distribution.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies promotional options with limited application to KBV.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Discusses advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in KBV's context with some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Evaluates all three options in context and recommends influencer marketing, explaining why television and radio are rejected.

questions.question_text: KBV's bottling-line defects are 2.4% and its labour turnover is 9%. Explain two benefits for KBV of using democratic leadership to improve motivation in its production team.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Democratic leadership gives the 40 employees a real voice in how the new automated bottling line is run, which helps satisfy social and esteem needs and raises job satisfaction. Workers who help set sealing routines and shift patterns are more likely to attend consistently, directly attacking KBV's 9% labour turnover and reducing disruption to the 60,000-unit output plan. This suits the flat organisational structure and keeps decision-making close to the people handling the bottles.

Point 2: Consulting operators produces practical ideas for reducing the 2.4% defect rate, because those staff see the sealing machines daily. Involvement builds commitment, so fewer skilled workers leave and KBV avoids repeatedly spending $800 per employee on off-the-job courses for the 12 of 40 staff still needing training. Higher commitment also protects the $7.00 contribution per unit and the $720,000 investment by keeping quality stable while the new line beds in, rather than relying on autocratic instructions that can breed resentment.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit of democratic leadership (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation linked to KBV's 2.4% defects, 9% turnover and training costs.

questions.question_text: KBV must upskill 12 production staff to operate the new bottling machines. Consider on-the-job training or off-the-job training at the local college. Which should KBV choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
On-the-job training: Coaching at the bottling line is directly relevant to KBV's own machines and quality standards, costs no course fees and keeps the 12 staff productive while they learn. This protects the 15,000 units packed last quarter and the effort already made to cut defects from 3.6% to 2.4%. The weaknesses are that trainers are themselves production workers whose output suffers, bad habits may be passed on, and there is little formal certification, which could matter if supermarket auditors request records.

Off-the-job training: The local college course at $800 per employee costs $9,600 for all 12 staff — small beside the $720,000 investment — and provides structured, up-to-date skills with a recognised certificate. It also removes 12 of 40 workers from the line for a period, cutting short-term capacity and risking the 9% labour-turnover situation worsening; the generic content may not match KBV's exact machine settings, so follow-up coaching would still be needed.

Decision: KBV should choose on-the-job training for the initial rollout, with short college top-ups later for senior operators. It is cheaper, machine-specific and avoids further output loss while defects are still 2.4%. Full off-the-job training is rejected because paying $9,600 and withdrawing 12 staff from a 40-person workforce would disrupt supermarket deliveries; college sessions can be added once the line is stable.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Describes the two training methods with limited KBV context.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses benefits and drawbacks of one or both methods in KBV's context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Evaluates both methods in context with a justified decision covering cost, disruption and machine relevance.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how KBV's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.
questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 35,000 units | (ii) Contribution per unit = $7.00 | (iii) Four applied uses: margin of safety of 25,000 units; discount pricing against $245,000 fixed costs; servicing the $450,000 loan; unit-cost benchmarking at $13.28.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $245,000 ÷ ($16.20 − $9.20) = $245,000 ÷ $7.00 = 35,000 units. Answer: break-even output is 35,000 units a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $16.20 − $9.20 = $7.00. Answer: contribution per unit is $7.00.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways KBV's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. Managers can compare the 35,000-unit break-even output with actual output of 60,000 units, giving a margin of safety of 25,000 units, to judge how safely the new bottling line can operate.
2. Contribution of $7.00 lets them model a retailer discount; for example a $0.50 cut would leave $6.50 per bottle, still above the level needed to cover $245,000 fixed costs.
3. The figures set volume targets for servicing the $450,000 bank loan taken for the $720,000 expansion.
4. Average total cost of $245,000 ÷ 60,000 + $9.20 = $13.28 a unit can be benchmarked each quarter to monitor the 2.4% bottling defect rate and the 9.3% input-cost inflation.

working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula/method and 1 mark for the accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii); 1 mark for each valid applied use in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate KBV's liquidity by calculating the current ratio and the acid test ratio for 2024 and 2025. Has KBV's liquidity improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Current Ratio 2024 = 1.42 : 1
Current Ratio 2025 = 1.58 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2024 = 0.70 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2025 = 0.92 : 1

Detailed workings: 2024 current assets = $150,000 inventories + $110,000 trade receivables + $38,000 cash = $298,000; 2025 current assets = $132,000 + $128,000 + $55,000 = $315,000. The 2024 figure divided by $210,000 current liabilities gives 1.42, and the 2025 figure divided by $200,000 gives 1.58. Excluding inventories: 2024 = ($298,000 − $150,000) ÷ $210,000 = 0.70; 2025 = ($315,000 − $132,000) ÷ $200,000 = 0.92.

Evaluation: Liquidity has strengthened on both measures. The current ratio rose from 1.42 to 1.58 because current assets grew by $17,000 while current liabilities fell by $10,000, so short-term obligations are covered more comfortably. The acid test rose from 0.70 to 0.92, meaning KBV is less dependent on selling wine inventories to pay debts — important while it services a $450,000 bank loan and has committed $720,000 to new equipment. The stronger acid test is the more convincing evidence of real improvement because it excludes stock that may be slow to sell if bottling defects persist at 2.4%. However, trade receivables increased from $110,000 to $128,000, tying up cash with supermarket customers, and cash of $55,000 is still small relative to $200,000 liabilities, so a late payment could weaken the position quickly.

Conclusion: KBV's liquidity has improved. Both measures are higher and the improvement does not rely on inventories, though rising receivables mean management should tighten credit control before further borrowing.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures with little or no accurate ratio calculation.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Calculates both ratios for both years accurately with contextual comment on the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate ratios for both years, detailed evaluation of inventories, receivables and liabilities, and a justified conclusion on liquidity.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for KBV of offering sustainably bottled wine.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: Market research of 500 shoppers found 68% would pay up to $0.50 more for sustainably bottled wine and 47% check bottle recycling before buying. Capturing that premium would lift revenue per bottle from $16.20 toward $16.70 and protect the $7.00 contribution per unit against the 9.3% rise in glass and cork input costs. It also differentiates KBV's wine on national supermarket shelves, supporting demand for the 60,000 units needed to justify the $720,000 bottling investment.

Disadvantage: Sustainable glass and closures can cost more than standard packaging, and the insert does not separate the $9.20 variable cost into components, so the exact increase cannot be quantified; if suppliers pass on higher charges, contribution would fall unless the $0.50 premium is accepted across the range. Any breakage or shorter shelf life would also aggravate the current 2.4% defect rate and raise waste before the new line stabilises, while the $450,000 bank loan still requires cash.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual development using KBV's survey data, costs and defects.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the interest rate rise to 5.0%, the 5.8% minimum wage increase and the 9.3% rise in glass and cork input costs will affect KBV. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Interest rate rise (4.25% to 5.0%): If KBV's $450,000 ten-year bank loan is variable-rate, the additional cost is 0.75% of $450,000 = $3,375 a year (0.0075 × $450,000). That is modest against $245,000 fixed costs, and if the loan is fixed-rate the immediate effect is nil. Higher rates may also make consumers more cautious about premium wine and raise the cost of any future borrowing, but KBV can largely control this by fixing the loan rate.

Minimum wage increase (5.8%, to $13.75 an hour): With a workforce of 40, a wage rise feeds into costs and cannot be avoided. The insert gives neither hours worked nor individual pay, so no annual wage total is defensible. The honest test is productivity: 60,000 units ÷ 40 staff = 1,500 units a worker, so the rise is affordable only if productivity holds or output grows; otherwise unit labour cost rises and the $7.00 contribution shrinks.

Input-cost inflation (9.3% glass and cork): The insert does not decompose the $9.20 variable cost, so only a bound can be shown: if the whole $9.20 rose 9.3% that adds $0.86 a unit (0.093 × $9.20), or about $51,000 a year at 60,000 units. Even a smaller pass-through would cut contribution materially, though the $0.50 eco-premium and retailer negotiations can recover part of it.

Conclusion: The 9.3% input-cost rise will have the greatest impact: it applies to every one of the 60,000 bottles and directly erodes the $7.00 contribution that underpins the $720,000 investment, whereas the interest rise is quantifiable and small and the wage effect depends on unstated hours. It is also harder for KBV to offset than the other two changes.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external changes with limited application to KBV.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two changes on KBV's costs, revenue or finance in context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Evaluates all three changes in context, concludes input-cost inflation is greatest and explains why the others are smaller.
